q-67810.name: Question 3
q-67810.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14173511/assets/944d21cd412d833271ca4c1939608055405df0695a4d2a6e1a3d8dedc9bed880.png)

Solve for $x$ in the figure above given that $\overset{⟷}{JK}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overset{―}{HI}.$
q-67810.worked_solution:
By the perpendicular bisector theorem, a point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment. Hence, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}IK & =HK \\ 6x & =x+15 \\ 5x & =15 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

q-76792.name: Question 5
q-76792.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14173511/assets/b365c6a6ae3ff9320465fe9a69e55b1737a7ffedf6cf6da6e91a5ed4ace3ba38.png)

Solve for $x$ in the figure above given that $PR=QR$ and $\overset{⟷}{RS}⊥\overset{―}{PQ}.$
q-76792.worked_solution:
By the converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem, a point equidistant from the endpoints of a segment lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment. 

Here, the point $R$ is equidistant from the endpoints of $\overset{―}{PQ}.$ Therefore, $\overset{⟷}{SR}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overset{―}{PQ}.$ 

In particular, we have that $SP=SQ.$ We can use this equation so solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}SP & =SQ \\ 8x-5 & =6x+1 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

q-67780.name: Question 7
q-67780.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14173511/assets/4b89ec998b55eacb8e5de3bf0c22aa94d351232f38459c17640956f96e939bac.png)

Solve for $x$ in the figure above given that $KN=LN$ and $KP=LP.$
q-67780.worked_solution:
By the converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem, a point equidistant from the endpoints of a segment lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment. 

Here, the points $P$ and $N$ are both equidistant from the endpoints of $\overset{―}{KL}.$ Therefore, $P$ and $N$ both  lie on the perpendicular bisector of $\overset{―}{KL}.$ 

Since only one line can be drawn through two given points, the line $\overset{⟷}{PN}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overset{―}{KL}.$ 

In particular, we have that $KM=LM.$ We can use this equation to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}KM & =LM \\ 8x-6 & =7x+1 \\ x & =7\end{aligned}
$$
